title: Coaching Case Studies #3
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton's third set of coaching reflections takes two maths lessons and mines each for a transferable principle. In the first, students calculating a mean on calculators produce the impossible answer 622.4; the teacher diagnoses on the spot that they divided only the final number by ten before adding, having not pressed equals. Barton's coaching point is not that the teacher erred but that she left value on the table: the wrong answer was an opportunity to put 622.4 to the whole class and ask both how we know instantly it cannot be right and how someone might have got it, since feasibility-checking and calculator use are themselves large maths issues. The second case rebuilds the standard routine for returning an exam paper. Barton names three problems with handing papers back first - ten minutes lost to score comparison, high-attaining students idle while struggling students still cannot see why they were wrong, and no way to know whether copying down the model equalled understanding. The redesign withholds the papers, models each troublesome question, then checks with a shadow-paper follow-up on mini-whiteboards. The twist is the real finding: every student got the first follow-up right and most got the second wrong, because the first follow-up was too close a clone and taught them to copy the method rather than think.
points: Barton's strongest coaching instinct here is that a diagnosed wrong answer should be handed back to the whole class as a thinking task, not just repaired with the two students who made it.
Asking both how we know an answer cannot be right and how someone might have produced it trains feasibility-checking, which he treats as a first-class maths skill alongside calculator technique.

The case against returning marked papers at the start of a lesson is operational and concrete: attention goes to scores for ten minutes, correct students have nothing to do, and wrong students still cannot self-diagnose.
Announcing in advance that a follow-up question is coming changed student behaviour during the explanation - engagement was bought by the promise of an imminent check, not by exhortation.

The failure of the second follow-up question is the most useful result: a shadow question that only swaps numbers teaches imitation, so it must be similar enough to test the same skill but different enough to require thought.
quotes: Students wrote their answers on their mini-whiteboards, and the teacher circulated the room offering feedback and support where needed. Most students got the correct answer of 68. But during circulation the teacher discovered that two students had an answer of 622.4.

Fortunately, the teacher was able to diagnose the issue on the spot: students had added the 10 numbers on their calculators, but not pressed equals before dividing by 10. Hence, as they follow the strict order of operations, their calculators had only divided the final number by 10 and then added that result onto the sum of the previous 9.

The feasibility of answers and correct use of a calculator are both big issues in maths and worthy of such consideration. Students who might make similar mistakes will certainly benefit from thinking about this explicitly, but even students who are secure with these ideas will benefit from trying to diagnose issues and then offer explanations.

It was a revision lesson for Year 11s. Students had just done a past paper which the teacher had marked. Her plan was to give the assessments back to the students, put the three worst answered questions on the board for students to have a go at, then go through them herself so the students could make corrections accordingly.
When the teacher models the correct solution, how does she know that the kids understand? Copying down does not equal learning.

Well, it went really well. The realisation that they were all going to be given a follow-up question meant that the students were all engaged in the explanation, and everyone then had a really good go at the follow-up questions.
